topic: Saggar: A Mac Terminal That Organizes Sessions

key_points: Saggar's own comparison page concedes the point up front: 'cmux and Saggar answer the same question and answer it in the same language... If you want a terminal built for agents and you want to read its source, the comparison is short: use cmux.'
The hardest competitor is a free, GPL-3.0 native Swift/AppKit app (cmux) versus Saggar's closed-source Mac-only app.

cmux strengths listed by Saggar itself: libghostty GPU-accelerated rendering that reads existing Ghostty config, notification rings on panes/tabs with an unread panel, vertical sidebar with branch + linked PR status + working directory + listening ports, built-in scriptable browser (accessibility-tree snapshot, click, form fill), CLI and Unix socket API, per-project cmux.json actions.

The claimed Saggar differentiator is a single ordered attention queue (prompts, failures, finished work) walked with Cmd+J, versus cmux's per-pane notification indicators; five statuses (needs you, working, idle, finished, failed) re-read every two seconds.

Second differentiator: first-party iPhone/remote client included with pairing gated on account + explicit approval on the Mac, where cmux's iOS app sits behind the paid Founder's Edition and TestFlight.
Project state is written to .saggar/ beside the code (scratchpad, commands, layouts, scheduled tasks) so agents working in that repo can read it.
Page carries the disclaimer 'Claims about cmux come from its own documentation and were last checked in August 2026' and has an explicit 'Pick cmux' verdict block.

Independent review framing the whole category: running three Claude Code instances, a Codex agent and Gemini CLI in parallel tmux panes 'works, but it's held together with duct tape. You can't tell which agent is waiting for input, which one finished, or which one hit an error without manually checking every pane.'
cmux launched February 2026, reached 26.6k GitHub stars by late August 2026, v0.64.22 on 2026-08-03; license moved from AGPL to GPL-3.0-or-later with a commercial option.

Named cmux weaknesses a reviewer can test Saggar against: macOS only, no live session restore on relaunch, very young (expect rough edges), occasional sandbox conflicts with agents, smaller ecosystem than tmux.

Feature detail: GPU rendering via libghostty, vertical tabs, agent notification rings (green complete / yellow waiting / red error), embedded scriptable browser, CLI + socket API, Ghostty config drop-in, Catppuccin themes.
Verdict line worth quoting: 'The agent notifications alone justify the switch for anyone running parallel Claude Code or Codex sessions on macOS.'

Frames the 2026 market in three tiers: purpose-built agentic terminals (Warp, cmux), high-performance general terminals (Ghostty, WezTerm, Kitty, iTerm2, Wave) with no agent awareness, and multiplexers (tmux, Zellij) that layer persistence on top of any emulator.
Saggar belongs to the first tier but is not listed by this guide at all — evidence the category survey is still cmux/Warp-led.
cmux positioning detail: shipping v0.64.10 (23.5.2026), 20,300 GitHub stars at time of writing, agent-agnostic (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Kiro, Aider).

tmux remains 'the de facto infrastructure for the entire multi-agent ecosystem': dmux (1,600+ stars) creates tmux panes with automatic git worktree creation, Claude Squad (7,700+ stars) manages multiple agent sessions, ccmanager (1,100+ stars) supports 8+ agent CLIs with session state detection.
Practical framing for a review: the decision is driven by how many parallel sessions you run and whether sessions must survive disconnection.

Explains the mechanism behind attention features: cmux's notification system works through OSC escape sequences (OSC 9, OSC 99, OSC 777) that agents emit and the terminal intercepts and turns into a blue pane ring, a lit sidebar tab, and an optional macOS notification.

Saggar's docs describe a different mechanism — process-tree walking plus an on-screen chrome scan, with opt-in provider hooks for starts/prompts/turns/exits — which is the technically interesting contrast to write up.
Notes cmux's browser automation is a port of agent-browser's accessibility tree API into WebKit/Swift, driven over a Unix socket at /tmp/cmux.sock with JSON commands (browser.interact, click, etc.).
Skip criteria stated plainly: Linux/Windows, teams needing cross-platform consistency, or anyone who needs a decade of plugins and StackOverflow answers.

Pricing and platform facts for the review's spec box: Free native Mac terminal manager; optional Pro remote control at GBP 1.99 / USD 2.50 per month with the first month free; macOS 26.0 or later on Apple Silicon; developer credited as Max Clayton Clowes.
Product one-liner to test against the official copy: 'A native Mac terminal manager built around one question: which session needs you now.'
States the Mac app needs no account and that a fresh install sends nothing off the Mac.
Names the target agents as Claude Code, Codex CLI, or Antigravity across several repos.

The Show HN thread itself (17 Aug 2026, 70 points, 21 comments) is the best source of real friction and is more useful than any marketing page: skeptics about running an unknown developer's binary, a broken signup flow (confirmation email never arriving, CSP blocking the site's own captcha, a 404 GitHub repo link), and a remote-relay trust objection.

Founder (mcclowes) replies inline to nearly every objection and confirms fixes as they land — signup restored, multi-Mac pairing added within the thread ('there's was only a small bit of code forcing 1-1 pairing so this SHOULD work now'), then a user confirming it works.

Platform objection to quote: 'Requires macOS 26 Tahoe or later — Why? Tahoe hasn't even reached its first birthday and plenty of us are still on Sequoia... There's nothing a terminal needs from Tahoe specifically.' The founder answers that macOS 26 is simply his lowest build/test target and says he will look at lowering it.

Remote-control security objection: 'The remote control appears to use a third party relay, and I don't see encryption mentioned. I really want to use this, but I definitely don't trust a vibe coded relay to my shell.' Founder: the third party is Cloudflare and it is encrypted.
Apple-Silicon-only objection and the answer: other OS builds are not ruled out, but Electron is explicitly rejected.

stats.fact: The Show HN launch of Saggar (17 Aug 2026) drew 70 points and 21 comments.

Saggar's closest competitor cmux sits at 27,532 GitHub stars (repo created 2026-01-28, last pushed 2026-10-01), i.e. roughly 8 months old and an order of magnitude more visible than a 70-point Show HN.
cmux launched February 2026 and had reached 26.6k GitHub stars by late August 2026, shipping v0.64.22 on 2026-08-03.
Agent use at work has nearly doubled in a year: 59% of surveyed developers use AI agents at any frequency in the April 2026 pulse survey, up from 31% in the 2025 Developer Survey.

Supervision, not autonomy, is the norm: 63% of technologists rarely or never let agents run entirely on autopilot, 60% block agents from making unapproved system changes, and 68% prefer predictable single-agent setups over complex multi-agent configurations.
stats.source: Stack Overflow pulse survey, 1,100 respondents, late April 2026 — https://stackoverflow.blog/2026/05/27/agents-on-a-leash-agentic-ai-remains-mostly-monitored-at-work/

stats.fact: Where multi-agent orchestration does happen it is daily and Claude-centric: daily multi-agent users use Claude Code the most (70%), while code-assistant usage overall is GitHub Copilot 61% and Claude Code 51%.

69% of AI agent users agree agents increased their productivity and ~70% agree agents reduced time spent on specific development tasks — the demand-side justification for tooling that keeps several agents supervised.
stats.source: 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, AI section — https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/ai

stats.fact: Only 17% of agent users agree agents improved collaboration within their team, the lowest-rated impact — supports the 'personal supervision tool, not team platform' angle.
stats.source: 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, AI section — https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/ai

stats.fact: Saggar pricing: the Mac app is free with no account; Pro is GBP 1.99 / USD 2.50 per month with the first month free and adds remote control, automations, queued sessions, local supervision decision history and push notifications.
Saggar requires a Mac on macOS 26 Tahoe or later on Apple Silicon; the vendor states plainly there is no Linux or Windows build and none is planned.
Saggar knows seven agent CLIs by name: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI, Pi, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code, with an 'Other agents' fallback.
Saggar is the companion app to Kiln, another Marginal Utility product, and is published as a native Swift/SwiftUI app built against macOS 26 rather than Electron.

angles: Review the category before the app: in 2026 a terminal is now an attention router, and Saggar is a bet that the scarce resource is your decision-making, not CPU or screen space. Use cmux's libghostty/notification-ring model as the incumbent to beat.

The 'supervision loop' as the review's spine: start work across projects, leave working agents alone, handle what needs you, step away without losing the thread. Test each of the four claims against the product rather than restating the marketing.

Mechanism deep-dive: Saggar classifies agent sessions two independent ways — a process-tree walk under each shell (claude, codex, agy, pi, opencode, copilot) plus an on-screen chrome scan when the walk fails — with opt-in provider hooks for starts, prompts, turns and exits. Contrast with cmux's OSC 9/99/777 escape-sequence notification rings.

The honest-comparison angle: the vendor's own compare page tells you to use cmux if open source or Ghostty config compatibility matters. Quoting that is rare and disarming, and it sharpens the review's verdict instead of softening it.

Attention queue versus status indicators: one ordered Cmd+J queue over prompts, failures and finished work, five statuses re-read every two seconds, versus per-pane rings and unread badges. This is the single most defensible differentiator to verify in practice.

Remote supervision as the paid boundary: the Mac app is genuinely free (no account, nothing leaves the Mac); Pro's only real addition is leaving the desk. Test whether 'queue work behind active sessions, answer a prompt from your phone' is worth USD 2.50/month — and note that remote control needs the Mac awake, online and running Saggar.

The security review a reviewer must not skip: pairing is account-gated with an explicit Mac approval and does not expire through inactivity; the Mac dials out to a Cloudflare relay and opens no inbound port; traffic is end-to-end sealed so the relay routes envelopes it cannot read; signing out on the Mac revokes every device. Then weigh the founder's 'vibe coded' build against the HN scepticism about trusting a shell to an unknown developer.

Rough-edges angle, sourced from the launch thread rather than the site: broken signup (confirmation emails, CSP blocking the site's own captcha, a 404 GitHub link) on launch day, macOS 26 Tahoe/Apple-Silicon-only with the founder saying Tahoe is merely his lowest build target, and a single closed-source app where the nearest rival is GPL-3.

Fit-and-misfit verdict logic: strong fit for macOS developers running three or more agent sessions across repos who lose track of which one stopped; weak fit for Linux/Windows, teams requiring cross-platform consistency, tmux-plus-SSH persistence shops, and anyone who needs to read the source.

Market timing with real numbers: 59% of developers now use agents (up from 31%), but 63% rarely or never let them run on autopilot and 68% prefer single-agent setups — Saggar's premise of supervised, human-in-the-loop agent work sits exactly on the mainstream behaviour, while full orchestration is still the minority case.

Where it sits versus four different rivals, not one: cmux (free open-source agent terminal), Warp (cloud orchestration platform), tmux/dmux/Claude Squad (cross-platform multiplexer ecosystem), and the vendor's own .saggar/ project-state convention that lets agents in the repo read scratchpad, commands, layouts and scheduled tasks.
